questions.topic_text: Topic 1.13/1.14: Item-by-item comparison of cost and NRV; materials held for use written down to replacement cost only when the finished product they convert into will sell below cost

topics.topic_name: NRV of materials held for use or disposal
Comparison of Cost and Net Realisable Value

questions.why: Highest-ranked AS 2 topic (rank 40) and a 90% match to an ICAI Study Material question.
questions.question_html:
Mr. Jatin gives the following information relating to the items forming part of the inventory as on 31.03.2023. His enterprise produces product P using Raw Material X.

  1. 900 units of Raw Material X (purchased @ ₹100 per unit). Replacement cost of Raw Material X as on 31.03.2023 is ₹80 per unit.
  2. 400 units of partly finished goods in the process of producing P. Cost incurred till date is ₹245 per unit. These units can be finished next year by incurring additional cost of ₹50 per unit.
  3. 800 units of Finished goods P and total cost incurred is ₹295 per unit.

Expected selling price of product P is ₹280 per unit, subject to a payment of 5% brokerage on selling price.

Determine how each item of inventory will be valued as on 31.03.2023. Also calculate the value of total Inventory as on 31.03.2023.
questions.answer_html:
As per AS 2 (Revised) “Valuation of Inventories”, materials and other supplies held for use in the production of inventories are not written down below cost if the finished products in which they will be incorporated are expected to be sold at cost or above cost. However, when there has been a decline in the price of materials and it is estimated that the cost of the finished products will exceed net realizable value, the materials are written down to net realizable value. In such circumstances, the replacement cost of the materials may be the best available measure of their net realizable value. In the given case, selling price of product P is ₹266 and total cost per unit for production is ₹295.

Hence the valuation will be done as under:

  1. 900 units of raw material X will be written down to replacement cost as market value of finished product is less than its cost, hence valued at ₹80 per unit.
  2. 400 units of partly finished goods will be valued at ₹216 per unit i.e., lower of cost (₹245) or Net realizable value ₹216 (Estimated selling price ₹266 per unit less additional cost of ₹50).
  3. 800 units of finished product P will be valued at NRV of ₹266 per unit since it is lower than cost ₹295.

Valuation of Total Inventory as on 31.03.2023:

ParticularsUnitsCost (₹)NRV / Replacement cost (₹)Value = units × cost or NRV whichever is less (₹)
Raw material X9001008072,000
Partly finished goods40024521686,400
Finished goods P8002952662,12,800
Value of Inventory3,71,200
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is comparing raw material's own cost against its own replacement cost in isolation, instead of first checking whether the finished product it converts into (Product P) will sell below its own total cost – AS 2 only permits marking raw material down to replacement cost when that downstream test fails. It is also easy to compute net selling price by forgetting the 5% brokerage deduction, which changes both the partly-finished-goods NRV and the finished-goods valuation.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.9: Costs excluded from inventory cost - abnormal waste, storage, non-attributable admin overheads, selling/distribution

topics.topic_name: Exclusions from the cost of inventories

questions.why: Newest MTP in the corpus and a Category A question — 93% identical to a Study Material question.
questions.question_html: "In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred." Provide examples of such costs as per AS 2 (Revised) 'Valuation of Inventories'.
questions.answer_html: Examples of costs excluded from inventory cost and expensed as incurred: (a) abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs; (b) storage costs, unless required by the production process itself; (c) administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition; (d) selling and distribution costs.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees included all administrative overheads as excluded costs, without distinguishing those that do (production-related) vs. do not (general admin) contribute to bringing inventory to its present location and condition.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.3/1.6/1.14: Lower of cost and NRV; fixed overhead absorbed at normal capacity; raw material NRV-linked write-down via replacement cost

topics.topic_name: NRV of materials held for use or disposal

questions.why: An RTP that carries three mapped topics at once, including the rank-40 NRV topic.
questions.question_html:

Total fixed overhead for the year was ₹3,60,000 on a normal capacity of 36,000 units, while actual production has been 30,000 units.

Calculate the value of closing stock when: (i) Net Realisable Value of Finished Goods B is ₹500 per unit; (ii) Net Realisable Value of Finished Goods B is ₹380 per unit.

(i) When NRV of Finished Goods B is ₹500 per unit (above cost of ₹410, so both items valued at cost, lower of cost and NRV):

questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is absorbing fixed overhead on the actual 30,000 units produced (giving ₹12/unit) instead of the normal capacity of 36,000 units (₹10/unit), overstating the cost of Finished Goods B in both scenarios.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.9: Normal loss absorbed into the cost of remaining good units, abnormal loss quantified separately and expensed

topics.topic_name: Exclusions from the cost of inventories

questions.why: Normal versus abnormal loss, the most repeated AS 2 idea, at an 80% Study Material match.
questions.question_html:
Wooden Plywood Limited has a normal wastage of 5% in the production process. During the year 2024-25, the Company used 16,000 MT of Raw material costing ₹190 per MT. At the end of the year, 950 MT of wastage was in stock. The accountant wants to know how this wastage is to be treated in the books.

You are required to: (1) Calculate the amount of abnormal loss. (2) Explain the treatment of normal loss and abnormal loss [In the context of AS-2].
questions.answer_html:
As per AS 2 (Revised) 'Valuation of Inventories', abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognised as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. The normal loss will be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end.

Material used: 16,000 MT @ ₹190 = ₹30,40,000.

Normal Loss (5% of 16,000 MT) = 800 MT (included in calculation of cost of inventories).

Net quantity of material = 15,200 MT.

Abnormal Loss in quantity = (950 − 800) = 150 MT.

Abnormal Loss = ₹30,000 [150 units @ ₹200 (₹30,40,000/15,200)].

The amount of ₹30,000 (Abnormal loss) will be charged to the Profit and Loss statement.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A frequent mistake here is computing the cost per MT by dividing total material cost by the full 16,000 MT used (or by the 15,050 MT actually remaining after all wastage), instead of by the 15,200 MT net quantity remaining after only the normal loss is absorbed, which is the figure AS 2 requires for costing the abnormal loss.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.9: Abnormal waste excluded from inventory cost and expensed to P&L; normal waste absorbed into remaining good units' cost

topics.topic_name: Exclusions from the cost of inventories

questions.why: Category A: 93.5% identical to a Study Material question on excluded costs.
questions.question_html: In a production process, normal waste is 5% of input. 5,000 MT of input were put in process resulting in wastage of 300 MT. Cost per MT of input is ₹1,000. The entire quantity of waste and finished output is in stock at the year end. State with reference to Accounting Standard, how will you value the inventories in this case? What will be treatment for normal and abnormal waste?
questions.answer_html:
As per para 13 of AS 2 (Revised), abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognized as expenses in the period in which they are incurred.

In this case, normal waste is 250 MT and abnormal waste is 50 MT. The cost of 250 MT will be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end. The cost of abnormal waste (50 MT × 1,052.6315 = ₹52,632) will be charged to the profit and loss statement.

Cost per MT (Normal Quantity of 4,750 MT) = 50,00,000 / 4,750 = ₹1,052.6315

Total value of inventory = 4,700 MT × ₹1,052.6315 = ₹49,47,368.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error is spreading the abnormal loss quantity into the cost-per-unit computation along with the normal loss, understating the abnormal loss charged to the profit and loss statement and correspondingly overstating closing inventory.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.9: Costs excluded from inventory valuation and expensed as incurred - abnormal waste, avoidable storage, non-contributing admin overheads, selling/distribution costs

topics.topic_name: Exclusions from the cost of inventories

questions.why: ICAI lifted this one from the Study Material verbatim (100% match) once already.
questions.question_html: "In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred." Provide examples of such costs as per AS 2 (Revised) 'Valuation of Inventories'.
questions.answer_html:
In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. Examples of such costs are:

(a) Abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs;

(b) Storage costs, unless the production process requires such storage.

(c) Administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition.

(d) Selling and distribution costs.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: Some examinees who selected this theory alternative listed only one or two of the four categories of cost excluded from inventory valuation under AS 2, most often omitting the distinction between avoidable and production-necessary storage costs.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.9: Abnormal waste excluded from inventory cost and expensed; normal loss absorbed into remaining good units' cost

topics.topic_name: Exclusions from the cost of inventories

questions.why: The abnormal-waste computation in its most examined form, 80% Study Material match.
questions.question_html: Wooden Plywood Limited has a normal wastage of 5% in the production process. During the year 2023-24, the Company used 16,000 MT of Raw material costing ₹190 per MT. At the end of the year, 950 MT of wastage was in stock. The accountant wants to know how this wastage is to be treated in the books. You are required to: (1) Calculate the amount of abnormal loss. (2) Explain the treatment of normal loss and abnormal loss in the context of AS-2.
questions.answer_html:
(i) As per AS 2 'Valuation of Inventories', abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour and other production costs are excluded from cost of inventories and such costs are recognised as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. The normal loss will be included in determining the cost of inventories (finished goods) at the year end.

(ii) Material used 16,000 MT @ ₹190 = ₹30,40,000. Normal Loss (5% of 16,000 MT) = 800 MT (included in calculation of cost of inventories). Net quantity of material = 15,200 MT.

(iii) Abnormal Loss in quantity (950 − 800) = 150 MT. Abnormal Loss = ₹30,000 [150 units @ ₹200 (₹30,40,000/15,200)]. The amount of ₹30,000 (Abnormal loss) will be charged to the Profit and Loss statement.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: A common error here is computing the abnormal loss quantity against the gross 16,000 MT used rather than against the 800 MT normal-loss benchmark, or valuing the abnormal loss at the original ₹190/MT purchase rate instead of the higher ₹200/MT rate that results once the normal loss is absorbed into the remaining good units.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.14: Finished goods at lower of cost and NRV; feeding raw material written down to replacement cost once FG NRV falls below cost

topics.topic_name: NRV of materials held for use or disposal

questions.why: The most recent AS 2 question actually set in a PYQ, on the rank-40 topic.
questions.question_html: SR Limited manufactures finished goods 'MP' from raw material 'RP'. Year ended 31st March 2025: Opening Inventory MP 4,000 units ₹1,20,000; RP 4,400 units ₹52,800. Purchase of RP 40,000 units ₹4,80,000. Labour ₹3,23,200. Fixed Overheads ₹3,15,000. Sales 40,200 units ₹11,20,000. Closing Inventory: MP 4,200 units; RP 4,000 units. Expected production 45,000 units of MP. Due to fall in market demand, sales price of MP fell to ₹22/unit; replacement cost of RP ₹11.50/unit on closing day. Calculate the value of Closing Stock of 'MP' and 'RP' as on 31st March 2025.
questions.answer_html:
W.N.1 Actual production: Sales 40,200 + Closing FG 4,200 − Opening FG 4,000 = 40,400 units.

W.N.2 RP consumed: Opening RP 4,400 + Purchases 40,000 = 44,400 available; less Closing RP 4,000 = 40,400 units consumed (1 unit RP per unit MP produced).

W.N.3 Cost per unit RP (weighted average): (Opening value 52,800 + Purchases 4,80,000) / 44,400 units = 5,32,800/44,400 = ₹12.00/unit.

Cost of Material Consumed (40,400 × ₹12)4,84,800
Direct Labour3,23,200
Fixed Overhead (3,15,000 × 40,400/45,000 — based on normal/expected production, not actual)2,82,800
Cost of Production10,90,800
Cost per unit (10,90,800/40,400)₹27
Net Realisable Value per unit (selling price)₹22

Since NRV (₹22) is less than cost (₹27), the closing MP inventory is valued at NRV. Since finished goods NRV is below cost, the raw material RP feeding it is valued at replacement cost (₹11.50), per AS 2's write-down rule.

Value of closing inventory: MP (4,200 × ₹22) = ₹92,400. RP (4,000 × ₹11.50) = ₹46,000.
questions.mistake_text: Examiner’s Comment: The performance of examinees in this part was not satisfactory. A majority of them were unable to determine the value of closing inventory of finished goods (MP) and raw materials (RP) in accordance with AS 2 "Valuation of Inventories". Several examinees failed to compute the cost of production correctly, particularly where certain items required proportionate allocation. Many could ascertain only the labour cost of ₹3,23,200, while the remaining elements of cost were incorrectly computed. Further, a large number of examinees valued the closing stock of finished goods (on NRV basis) and raw materials (on replacement cost basis) incorrectly.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.6/1.7: Costs of conversion allocated between joint products on a rational basis (relative sales value), with by-product/scrap net realisable value deducted from the joint cost pool before allocation

Well Wear Limited is a Textile Manufacturing Company and engaged in the production of Polyester (P) and Nylon (N). While manufacturing the main products, a by-product Fiber (F) is also produced. Details of the cost of production are as under:

On the basis of the above information, you are required to compute the value of closing inventory of Polyester and Nylon.

questions.topic_text: Topic 1.11/1.12: Retail/gross-margin method of cost estimation; NRV of defective stock
questions.why: Latest MTP, and the only recent hit on the retail method and NRV estimation.
questions.question_html:
In the following cases, find the value of closing stock as per AS 2:
(i) Sonu is a retailer dealing in toys. During the year, he purchased items worth for ₹1,47,000 and made a total sale ₹1,54,000. The average percentage of gross margin is 10% on cost. Opening stock of toys at cost was ₹20,000.
(ii) On 21st March, 2026, Mohan purchased 250 chairs at ₹300 each. The selling price of the chair is ₹400 each. Owing to a manufacturing defect, net realisable value of the whole lot of chair was determined at 70% of their normal selling price. No chairs were sold during the year. (4 Marks)
questions.answer_html:
(i) Cost of closing inventory is shown below:

Sale value of opening stock and purchases (₹20,000 + ₹1,47,000) x 1.101,83,700
Sales(1,54,000)
Sale value of unsold stock29,700
Less: Gross Margin (₹29,700/1.10) x 0.10(2,700)
Cost of closing inventory27,000

Alternative presentation

Opening stock and purchases (₹20,000 + ₹1,47,000)1,67,000
Less: cost of goods sold(1,40,000)
Cost of closing inventory27,000

Calculation of cost of goods sold:

Goods sold1,54,000
Less: gross margin (1,54,000 x 10/110)(14,000)
Cost of goods sold1,40,000

(ii)

Closing stock at cost (250 x ₹300) (i)75,000
Net Realizable value of closing stock (₹280* x 250) (ii)70,000
Value of closing stock [lower of (i) and (ii)]70,000

*₹280 = 70% of ₹400 selling price.
questions.mistake_text: Author’s Note: Several examinees applied the gross margin percentage directly to sales value instead of grossing up cost through the margin percentage, producing an incorrect closing stock figure in part (i) under AS 2; in part (ii), some compared cost against the normal selling price instead of the defect-adjusted net realisable value.
